claims.text: The baseline refractory high-entropy alloy is produced by conventional powder metallurgy and has minimal intrinsic oxide dispersion.
A minor yttrium addition under controlled oxygen availability will promote in-situ formation of fine oxide particles.
The in-situ oxide particles will be nanoscale and distributed both at grain boundaries and within grains.
The oxide dispersoids will pin dislocations.
The oxide dispersoids will pin grain boundaries.
Dislocation and grain-boundary pinning will reduce high-temperature creep.
Dislocation and grain-boundary pinning will increase elevated-temperature yield strength.
The yttrium-modified alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength than the baseline alloy without a reactive-element addition.
The yttrium-modified alloy will have greater creep resistance than the baseline alloy.
The yttrium addition and resulting oxide dispersion will not appreciably increase alloy density.
The modification will leave room-temperature mechanical properties largely unchanged.
The modification will not appreciably degrade room-temperature ductility.
The predicted strengthening and creep benefit is expected at temperatures above 800 °C under sustained loading.
The benefit requires an optimized reactive-element addition that produces fine, stable oxides.
Excessive oxide coarsening could nullify the mechanical improvement.
Unwanted phase transformations caused by processing deviations or excessive addition could nullify the improvement.
The magnitude of strengthening and creep-resistance enhancement depends on the alloy composition and processing parameters.
